items.title: ChatGPT Dots vs Hermes Agent: Paid vs Free
items.content:
ChatGPT Dots vs Hermes is really a question of philosophy. Dots are OpenAI’s polished, paid, always-on agents living inside ChatGPT. Hermes Agent is the free, open-source agent I run my whole operation on, living on my own machine with whatever model I choose. When I tested Dots on launch day (above), my honest reaction was that it feels like “a version of Hermes Agent for beginners that’s still not that smooth.” Here’s the full comparison.

Key takeaways

- Dots: paid, managed, beginner-friendly — GPT-6 Astra, own cloud computer, 4,000+ apps, inside ChatGPT.

- Hermes: free and open source — runs on your machine, any model (local or cloud), bot mode, Bot Screen, voice.

- Control: Hermes gives you everything — models, data, plugins; Dots gives you Custom Rules within OpenAI’s walls.

- My take: Dots is easier to start; Hermes is more capable, cheaper and yours.

## ChatGPT Dots vs Hermes in practice

Dots win on first-run experience: open ChatGPT, name your Dot, pick an avatar, done. For someone who’s never touched an agent, that matters. But in my test the experience fell apart on real work — slow computer use, a call feature that didn’t connect, images that wouldn’t load, and app connections hidden away.

Hermes asks more of you up front, then gives you more: pick the best model for each job, run it locally for privacy, watch it on its own screen, talk to it hands-free, and keep every session in your own vault. No regional restrictions, no plan tiers, no waiting for a beta to settle. That’s why I run my business on it.

## Who should pick which

- Never used an agent, happy to pay, outside Europe: Dots is the gentlest start.

- Want control, privacy or zero subscription: Hermes, no contest.

Early-rollout bugs (like the call button) may be fixed quickly — I’ll update this page as they are.

## The bottom line on ChatGPT Dots vs Hermes

ChatGPT Dots vs Hermes: Dots is the easy, paid, managed option that’s still rough on day one; Hermes is the free, open, more capable agent you control completely. If you’re willing to spend an hour on setup, Hermes wins — and it doesn’t care what plan or country you’re in. Full Dots review: ChatGPT Dots, tested.

## Where ChatGPT Dots vs Hermes is closer than it looks

To be fair to Dots, a few things it ships on day one take real work to match in Hermes. Its Custom Rules give non-technical users a clean approval model — act alone, act if pre-approved, ask first, or escalate — and sensitive actions like password changes always need your sign-off. It connects to 4,000+ apps through OpenAI’s plugin ecosystem, keeps memories between conversations, and you can message your Dot from ChatGPT on desktop, web or mobile, with Slack and Teams too.

Hermes can do all of that — approvals through your config, integrations through its connectors and MCP servers, memory through your own vault — but you assemble it rather than switch it on. So the honest framing is: Dots trades control and cost for convenience. If convenience is what you’re short of, that trade can make sense; if control or budget matters more, Hermes is the better long-term home.

Dots are paid, managed always-on agents inside ChatGPT running on OpenAI’s cloud; Hermes is a free, open-source agent that runs on your own machine with any model you choose.

Yes — it’s open source and free to run; you only pay if you choose paid model APIs or subscriptions.

Yes to start: Dots set up in minutes inside ChatGPT. Hermes takes more setup but gives far more control and capability.

Yes — Hermes bot mode runs always-on on your machine, and Bot Screen lets you watch it work.

### Which is better for privacy?

Hermes — it runs locally and can use local models, so your data doesn’t have to leave your machine.

### Can I use ChatGPT Dots outside the US?

Pro access excludes the EU/EEA, Switzerland and the UK at launch; Business Premium works in all ChatGPT regions.

items.title: ChatGPT Dots: Is OpenAI’s New Agent Worth It?
items.content:
ChatGPT Dots are OpenAI’s answer to always-on AI agents — launched at DevDay on 29 September 2026, each Dot gets its own cloud computer and browser, can connect to 4,000+ apps, and keeps working after you close the tab. I set one up on day one and put it through real tasks (that’s the video above): research, a website, its own computer, even booking a restaurant. Some of it genuinely works. A lot of it is slow, and a couple of headline features didn’t work at all. Here’s what Dots are, who can get them, my honest results, and whether you should switch.

Key takeaways

- What they are: always-on agents inside ChatGPT, powered by GPT-6 Astra, each with its own cloud computer and browser and access to 4,000+ apps.

- Who can get them: ChatGPT Pro (not in the EU/EEA, Switzerland or the UK at launch) and Business Premium; Enterprise and Edu in admin-enabled beta.

- My test: research and site-building worked; computer use was very slow, the call button didn’t connect, and an avatar took 20–30 minutes.

- My verdict for now: not worth switching — Claude is faster for results, Grok Bot is smoother for computer use, Hermes is free and open.

## What ChatGPT Dots actually are

A Dot is an agent that lives inside ChatGPT and doesn’t stop when you do. You give it a name and an avatar, connect your apps, and hand it ongoing work; it runs on its own cloud computer (or, optionally, your local machine via the desktop app), keeps memories between conversations, and checks back when something needs you. OpenAI’s examples include monitoring customer feedback and preparing fixes, catching forgotten invoices, and turning interview transcripts into clips and posts.

Two design choices stand out. First, Custom Rules let you decide, per type of action, whether your Dot acts on its own, acts if pre-approved, asks first, or escalates to you — and sensitive actions like password changes always need approval. Second, it’s built for background work: while idle it can do proactive, read-only research across your connected apps. It’s the same “always-on agent” idea as Grok Bot and Hermes bot mode, packaged for mainstream ChatGPT users.

Credit where due: parallel tasks work, the takeover feature is handy (you grab control to log in or click something, then hand it back), and the restaurant booking did complete — it just opened the terms and conditions first and took about five minutes. ChatGPT Dots are a polished, beginner-friendly take on always-on agents, with sensible approval controls and genuinely useful research and site-building. items.content:
Jev 1.13 free is currently the easiest way to call TypeSafe’s Jev decision model from real code without paying: OpenCode Zen serves a limited-time `jev-1.13-free` model alongside the paid `jev-1.13`, on the same endpoint. It’s method three in my free-Jev video above. Here’s exactly how to use it, how it compares with the paid version, and how to make sure your workflows don’t break the day the free window closes.

Key takeaways

- Model ID `jev-1.13-free` on OpenCode Zen’s System One endpoint `https://opencode.ai/zen/v1/systemone` — free input and output, for a limited time.

- The paid twin `jev-1.13` is $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, on the same endpoint.

- You need an OpenCode Zen account and API key — billing details are required even though the free model costs nothing.

- No end date is published — build with an automatic fallback to paid jev-1.13 so nothing breaks.

## What Jev 1.13 free is

Jev is TypeSafe’s fast decision model: instead of writing paragraphs, it answers yes/no, choice and score questions in a fraction of a second (my Jev agent guide covers how). Version 1.13 is the build OpenCode Zen serves, and alongside the normal paid model it offers `jev-1.13-free` — the same endpoint, no charge, for a limited time.

This matters because the other big free route, the Vercel AI Gateway window, closed on 25 September 2026. For builders who want to test Jev in real workflows without a bill, jev-1.13-free is now the main door — alongside the no-code playground covered in my access guide.

## How to use Jev 1.13 free

- 1. Sign in to OpenCode Zen, add billing details, and copy your API key.

items.title: ChatGPT Dots vs Manus: Which Cloud Agent Is Better?
items.content:
ChatGPT Dots vs Manus pits OpenAI’s brand-new always-on agent against one of the original cloud-computer agents. Both give the AI its own computer in the cloud to do tasks for you. When I tested Dots on launch day (above), my verdict was that even Manus from three to six months ago was a better experience than what Dots delivered. Here’s the comparison and why maturity matters so much with agents.

Key takeaways

- Both run tasks on their own cloud computer and can work while you’re away.

- Manus’ advantage is maturity — it’s had many months of real-world use and iteration.

- Dots’ advantages: GPT-6 Astra, 4,000+ app connections, Custom Rules, and living inside ChatGPT.

- My take: for dependable cloud-computer tasks today, Manus; for ChatGPT-native convenience later, Dots.

The Dots experience I recorded was the classic first-release agent: good at research and site-building, but slow on its cloud computer (about two minutes before starting a search), a booking that took five minutes, a call feature that didn’t connect, and hidden app connections. Manus has already worked through many of those rough edges — which is why I said in the video that it would be the better choice, and was even months ago.

Dots may well catch up: OpenAI’s approval model (Custom Rules, auto-review, always-approve for sensitive actions) is thoughtful, and 4,000+ apps is a big head start on integrations. But agents are judged on whether tasks finish reliably, and that comes from iteration.

- Research briefs: Dots did this well — a step-by-step DevDay brief saved to its workspace. A good fit if you already live in ChatGPT.
